title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Ethical Practice, Client Rights & Advocacy
html:
Ethical nursing practice begins with the dignity and self-determination of the person receiving care. The RN provides accurate information within scope, protects privacy, recognizes coercion and unequal treatment, raises safety concerns, and supports decisions consistent with the client’s values—even when those decisions differ from the nurse’s preferences.

Learning goals

  • Apply foundational ethical principles to nursing situations.
  • Protect a capable client’s right to accept, refuse, or stop treatment.
  • Describe the RN’s responsibilities within the informed-consent process.
  • Distinguish decision-making capacity from legal competence.
  • Protect privacy, confidentiality, and appropriate information access.
  • Recognize ethical conflict and use an effective advocacy pathway.

Use ethical principles as a lens

  • Autonomy: support informed self-determination.
  • Beneficence: act to promote the client’s well-being.
  • Nonmaleficence: avoid or minimize preventable harm.
  • Justice: treat people fairly and distribute benefits and burdens using ethically relevant criteria.
  • Fidelity: keep professional commitments and maintain trust.
  • Veracity: communicate truthfully.

Principles may point in different directions. Naming the conflict helps the team examine facts, stakeholders, rights, likely harms, the client’s values, and possible actions rather than reducing a difficult choice to a slogan.

Center self-determination

A client with decision-making capacity has the right to receive understandable information, ask questions, choose among options, refuse treatment, and change a decision without coercion. Respecting autonomy does not mean abandoning the client. The RN assesses understanding and immediate safety, explores concerns without pressure, communicates the decision, continues appropriate care, and documents objectively.

Refusal is a cue for conversation—not permission for force
Determine what the client is refusing and why. Address pain, fear, language barriers, misinformation, access problems, or other reversible barriers; ensure the client understands likely consequences and alternatives; notify the responsible clinician; and follow policy. A capable, informed refusal remains the client’s decision.

Capacity is decision-specific

Clinical decision-making capacity concerns whether the client can understand relevant information, appreciate how it applies to the situation, reason about options, and communicate a choice. It can vary with the decision and change over time. Confusion, a psychiatric diagnosis, disability, disagreement, or an unwise choice does not automatically prove incapacity. Competence is a legal determination; terminology and processes vary by jurisdiction.

When the client lacks capacity, follow the applicable advance directive and legally authorized surrogate process. A surrogate represents the client’s known wishes or interests; the surrogate does not overrule a client who currently has capacity. Urgent emergencies, minors, guardianship, and specific treatments may have additional requirements.

Support informed consent

Informed consent is a communication and decision process, not merely a signature. The practitioner responsible for the proposed procedure or treatment generally explains its nature, purpose, material risks and benefits, reasonable alternatives, and the option of no treatment, according to law and policy. The RN reinforces information within scope, uses accessible communication and a qualified interpreter when needed, checks voluntariness and understanding, and advocates when questions remain.

When witnessing a signature, the RN follows organizational policy—commonly verifying identity, voluntariness, and that the signature was made by the appropriate person. Witnessing does not transfer responsibility for the procedural explanation to the RN and does not prove understanding. If the client is sedated, appears unable to decide, says the explanation was not understood, or asks unanswered questions, pause the process and notify the responsible practitioner.

Protect privacy and confidentiality

Privacy concerns the person’s control over access to body, space, and personal information. Confidentiality is the duty to safeguard information entrusted in the care relationship. Provide physical privacy, verify who may receive information, use approved communication channels, secure records and screens, and avoid discussing identifiable details where they can be overheard.

Access information only for an authorized work purpose and follow applicable privacy law and organizational policy regarding disclosure and the minimum necessary standard. Some rules have specific exceptions, including certain disclosures for treatment or required by law; do not invent an exception. Curiosity is never a clinical need. Never share client stories, photographs, recordings, or identifiable details on personal social media—even after removing a name if the person could still be recognized.

Maintain professional boundaries

The therapeutic relationship exists for the client’s benefit. Avoid exploiting trust, accepting inappropriate benefits, imposing personal beliefs, or shifting the client into caring for the nurse’s emotional needs. Use transparent, approved communication and ask for guidance when gifts, dual relationships, social media contact, or conflicts of interest create uncertainty.

Advocacy is a clinical action

Advocacy includes clarifying an unsafe or inconsistent order, obtaining language access, protecting a refusal, reporting a change, addressing discrimination, and ensuring that unresolved concerns reach someone able to act. State the specific facts, immediate risk, client’s wishes, and requested action. Use the chain of command when the first response does not resolve a significant safety or rights concern, and continue necessary protection within scope.

Work through ethical conflict

Identify the question precisely, gather clinical and contextual facts, determine the client’s current capacity and stated values, identify affected people and obligations, examine alternatives and foreseeable consequences, and consult appropriate resources. The charge nurse, responsible clinician, ethics service, risk management, privacy officer, social work, chaplaincy, interpreter services, and leadership may each have a role. Ethical consultation supports a fair process; it does not replace the capable client’s voice.

Moral distress can occur when the nurse believes the ethically appropriate action is constrained. Seek timely support, document clinical facts rather than accusations, use established reporting pathways, and maintain safe continuity of care. Personal objection does not permit abandonment; any transfer of care must be safe, timely, and consistent with professional obligations and policy.

Evaluate the advocacy outcome

After acting, determine whether the client received understandable information, privacy was restored, the refusal or preference was honored, the unsafe condition was corrected, and the plan now reflects the client’s goals. Continue escalation when a material concern remains unresolved. Document the assessment, communication, people notified, actions, client response, and follow-up without editorial or retaliatory language.

Clinical example

An alert client scheduled for a procedure says, “I signed because my family told me to, but I still do not understand the risks and I do not want to go.” The RN stops preparation that can safely be paused, assesses what the client understands, protects the client from pressure, notifies the procedural practitioner, arranges communication support if needed, and documents the client’s words and actions taken. The RN does not treat the signed form as permission to ignore a current refusal.
